items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the number of live births per 1000 people in a population per year”?
items.answer: Crude birth rate
items.markingKey: Crude birth rate: the number of live births per 1000 people in a population per year. [1]

items.stem: Explain why death rates have fallen in most countries since 1950.
items.answer: Improved health care, vaccination and antibiotics; clean water and sanitation; better nutrition and food supply; education about hygiene.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed reason up to [3]

items.stem: Explain why birth rates are high in many low-income countries.
items.answer: Children work on farms and support parents in old age; high infant mortality; limited access to contraception and education for women; early marriage; cultural and religious traditions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per reason up to [3]

items.stem: Table 5.1 shows birth and death rates (per 1000 per year) for selected countries. India: birth rate 15, death rate 7. Japan: birth rate 5, death rate 14. Germany: birth rate 9, death rate 12. Suggest the environmental pressures that a population growing as fast as India may face.
items.answer: Increased demand for farmland, fuelwood and water; deforestation, soil erosion and water stress; growth of informal settlements with poor sanitation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per pressure up to [2]

items.stem: Table 5.1 shows birth and death rates (per 1000 per year) for selected countries. Nigeria: birth rate 36, death rate 13. Egypt: birth rate 22, death rate 7. Japan: birth rate 6, death rate 12. Brazil: birth rate 11, death rate 6. (a) Using the rule of 70, estimate the doubling time of the population of Nigeria. (b) Suggest the environmental pressures that a population growing as fast as Nigeria may face.
items.answer: (a) About 30 years (b) Increased demand for farmland, fuelwood and water; deforestation, soil erosion and water stress; growth of informal settlements with poor sanitation.
items.markingKey: (a) 70 ÷ 2.3 [1] (b) 1 mark per pressure up to [2]

items.stem: To what extent is it true that rapid population growth is the main cause of environmental problems? In your answer you should consider: ecological footprint; I = PAT; named countries.
items.answer: For: More people increase demand for food, water and energy, causing deforestation, soil degradation and water stress (e.g. the Sahel). Against: Consumption per person matters more: high-income countries with slow growth have the largest ecological footprints; technology and governance determine impacts (I = PAT). Judgement: Population growth is one factor, but levels of consumption, technology and management are often more important.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 3 (6-8 marks): detailed, balanced discussion using named examples and data, with a reasoned judgement. Level 2 (3-5 marks): developed points but limited balance or exemplification. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generalised points. [8]

items.stem: Explain why the total fertility rate falls as women gain access to education and employment.
items.answer: Women marry later, have careers, understand and use contraception, and want fewer children who are more costly to educate; they have more say in family decisions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [3]

items.stem: Malaysia has a population of 22 million, a birth rate of 20 per 1000, a death rate of 6 per 1000 and a net migration rate of −3 per 1000 per year. (a) Calculate the total population change in one year, including migration. (b) Suggest one reason for the net migration figure.
items.answer: (a) +242 000 (b) Emigration for work and higher wages abroad (economic push factors).

items.stem: Table 5.1 shows birth and death rates (per 1000 per year) for selected countries. India: birth rate 15, death rate 6. Mexico: birth rate 15, death rate 7. Italy: birth rate 8, death rate 12. Brazil: birth rate 12, death rate 7. (a) Calculate the rate of natural increase (%) for each country. (b) Name a country in the table with natural decrease and suggest why. (c) Using the rule of 70, estimate the doubling time of the population of India.
items.answer: (a) India 0.9%; Mexico 0.8%; Italy −0.4%; Brazil 0.5% (b) Italy: very low birth rate and an ageing population with a relatively high death rate. (c) About 78 years
items.markingKey: (a) (birth rate − death rate) ÷ 10; two correct [1]; all correct [1] [2] (b) identification [1]; reason [1] [2] (c) 70 ÷ 0.9 [1]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a model showing how birth rates, death rates and total population change as a country develops, in five stages”?
items.answer: Demographic transition model (DTM)
items.markingKey: Demographic transition model (DTM): a model showing how birth rates, death rates and total population change as a country develops, in five stages. [1]

items.stem: Explain the shape of a population pyramid for a country in stage 2 of the DTM.
items.answer: A wide base because the birth rate is high; sides that narrow quickly and a narrow top because the death rate, though falling, is still relatively high and life expectancy is low.
items.markingKey: wide base / high births [1]; narrow top / low life expectancy [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain the problems that an ageing population may cause.
items.answer: Higher costs of pensions and health care; a shrinking workforce paying taxes; labour shortages; fewer people to care for the elderly; possibly slower economic growth.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed problem up to [3]

items.stem: In South Korea, 13% of the population is aged 0-14, 71% is aged 15-64 and 16% is aged 65 and over. Suggest one problem caused by this population structure and one way the government could respond.
items.answer: A growing working-age population needs jobs; invest in skills and industry.
items.markingKey: problem [1]; response [1] [2]

items.stem: In Niger, 50% of the population is aged 0-14, 46% is aged 15-64 and 4% is aged 65 and over. (a) Calculate the dependency ratio. (b) Describe the likely shape of the population pyramid.
items.answer: (a) 117.4 (b) Wide base narrowing rapidly towards a narrow top.

items.stem: In Indonesia, 24% of the population is aged 0-14, 69% is aged 15-64 and 7% is aged 65 and over. (a) Calculate the young and old dependency ratios separately. (b) Suggest which stage of the DTM the country is in. Give a reason.
items.answer: (a) young 34.8; old 10.1 (b) Stage 3, because a large proportion of the population is young, indicating high birth rates.

items.stem: “The demographic transition model is of limited use in understanding population change in low-income countries today.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? Refer to examples you have studied.
items.answer: For: It is based on 19th-century Europe; today death rates in LICs fell faster because of imported medicine; migration, HIV/AIDS and policies (China’s one-child policy) are not included. Against: It still describes the broad sequence seen in Bangladesh, Brazil and Iran, where falling death rates were followed by falling birth rates; it helps predict future needs. Judgement: The model is a useful general framework but must be adapted to each country’s circumstances.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 3 (6-8 marks): detailed, balanced discussion using named examples and data, with a reasoned judgement. items.stem: Explain the limitations of the demographic transition model.
items.answer: It is based on European experience; it does not include migration; it assumes all countries will follow the same path; it does not predict timing; some countries have skipped stages or been affected by AIDS or policies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per limitation up to [3]

items.stem: In Germany, 13% of the population is aged 0-14, 66% is aged 15-64 and 21% is aged 65 and over. (a) Describe the likely shape of the population pyramid. (b) Suggest one problem caused by this population structure and one way the government could respond.
items.answer: (a) Narrow base, wide middle and top (column or inverted shape). (b) Rising pension and health costs with fewer workers; raise the retirement age or encourage immigration.

items.answer: (a) young 16.9; old 23.9 (b) Fairly straight sides with a slightly narrower base than middle.

items.answer: (a) Stage 4, because there are few young people and a large elderly population, indicating low birth rates and high life expectancy. (b) Rising pension and health costs with fewer workers; raise the retirement age or encourage immigration.

items.stem: Explain the impacts of out-migration on rural areas in low-income countries.
items.answer: Loss of young, economically active people; fewer farm workers so land may be abandoned; ageing population and more women-headed households; remittances can improve incomes and housing; skills may return later.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed impact up to [3]

items.stem: In one year Australia (population 54 million) had 204 000 immigrants and 494 000 emigrants. Calculate the net migration rate per 1000 people.
Discuss whether the impacts of migration are greater for the source area than for the destination. Give arguments for and against.
items.answer: For: Source areas lose young workers and skills (brain drain), changing their population structures, but gain remittances (e.g. Nepal, about a quarter of GDP). Against: Destinations gain labour and taxes but face pressure on housing, services and the environment, especially in rapidly growing cities such as Lagos or Dhaka. Judgement: Impacts are significant at both ends; their balance depends on the scale and type of migration and how it is managed.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 3 (5-6 marks): well-developed points on both sides with examples and a supported conclusion. Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points, limited balance or example. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple statements. [6]

items.stem: Explain the environmental impacts of rapid rural-urban migration on cities.
items.answer: Growth of informal settlements on hazardous land; inadequate sanitation and waste collection polluting water; air pollution from traffic and industry; loss of farmland and habitats at the urban fringe.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed point up to [3]

items.stem: Explain why some governments introduce pro-natalist policies.
items.answer: Fertility below replacement level leads to population decline and ageing; fewer workers and taxpayers to support pensions and health care; concerns about economic growth and national security.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per reason up to [3]

items.stem: For China’s one-child policy (1979-2015) or another example of a population policy, briefly evaluate the success of the policy.
items.answer: China’s one-child policy (1979-2015): The fertility rate fell from about 2.8 to about 1.6 and an estimated 200-400 million births may have been prevented, though fertility was already falling; problems included a sex ratio of about 117:100, rapid ageing and a shrinking workforce, leading to a two-child policy in 2016 and three children in 2021.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. evidence of changes in fertility; side-effects; judgement [4]

items.stem: Name an example of a population policy. For your chosen example, describe the aims and methods of the policy.
items.answer: Model answer (China’s one-child policy (1979-2015)): To slow population growth and support economic development by limiting most urban couples to one child, using incentives for compliance and fines for extra births.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: named measures, incentives and penalties Level 3 (5-6 marks): well-developed points on both sides with examples and a supported conclusion. Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points, limited balance or example. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple statements. [6]

items.stem: Explain why pro-natalist policies often have limited success.
items.answer: The costs of raising children (housing, education), careers, later marriage and changing attitudes are hard to offset with payments; effects are often small and temporary.

items.answer: Humans use technology to increase resources, trade to import resources, and have very different levels of consumption; resource needs change over time.

items.stem: Table 5.5 shows ecological footprint and biocapacity per person (global hectares, gha): Indonesia footprint 1.7, biocapacity 1.3; India footprint 1.2, biocapacity 0.4; United Kingdom footprint 4.2, biocapacity 1.1. World biocapacity is about 1.6 gha per person. Suggest how a country can have a footprint larger than its biocapacity.
items.answer: It imports resources (food, timber, energy) from other countries, uses up stocks (fossil fuels, overfishing) and emits more CO₂ than its ecosystems absorb.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [2]

items.stem: Discuss whether the world is overpopulated. Give arguments for and against.
items.answer: For: Humanity’s ecological footprint exceeds biocapacity by about 70%; biodiversity loss, climate change and water stress suggest limits are being exceeded. Against: Food production has kept pace with population (Boserup); the problem is unequal consumption and distribution; fertility is falling and population may peak this century. Judgement: The world is not overpopulated in terms of numbers alone, but current levels of consumption are unsustainable.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 3 (5-6 marks): well-developed points on both sides with examples and a supported conclusion. Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points, limited balance or example. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple statements. [6]

items.stem: Explain why high-income countries have larger ecological footprints than low-income countries.

A positive feature of a place that attracts people, such as jobs, safety or better services.

items.stem: In India, 25% of the population is aged 0-14, 67% is aged 15-64 and 8% is aged 65 and over. Calculate the young and old dependency ratios separately.
items.answer: young 37.3; old 11.9

items.stem: Amara argues that the demographic transition model is of limited use in understanding population change in low-income countries today. Discuss this view, referring to named examples. In your answer you should consider: named countries; migration and policy.
items.answer: For: It is based on 19th-century Europe; today death rates in LICs fell faster because of imported medicine; migration, HIV/AIDS and policies (China’s one-child policy) are not included. Against: It still describes the broad sequence seen in Bangladesh, Brazil and Iran, where falling death rates were followed by falling birth rates; it helps predict future needs. Judgement: The model is a useful general framework but must be adapted to each country’s circumstances.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 4 (10-12 marks): detailed, balanced evaluation supported by named examples and a clear, justified conclusion. Level 3 (7-9 marks): developed discussion with examples, judgement partly supported. Level 2 (4-6 marks): some relevant points, mostly descriptive. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, unsupported statements. [12]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “push factor”?
options: A person forced to leave their country because of persecution, war or violence.
A negative feature of a place that encourages people to leave, such as unemployment, conflict or drought.
A positive feature of a place that attracts people, such as jobs, safety or better services.
A person forced to flee their home who remains within their own country.
items.answer: A negative feature of a place that encourages people to leave, such as unemployment, conflict or drought.
items.markingKey: Push factor: a negative feature of a place that encourages people to leave, such as unemployment, conflict or drought. [1]

items.stem: Explain the benefits of immigration for a host country with an ageing population.
items.answer: Migrants fill labour shortages, pay taxes that support pensions and health care, raise the birth rate and bring skills and cultural diversity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [3]

items.stem: In one year Australia (population 31 million) had 477 000 immigrants and 265 000 emigrants. (a) Calculate the net migration rate per 1000 people. (b) Describe one environmental impact of large-scale immigration into cities.
items.answer: (a) 6.8 per 1000 (b) Increased demand for housing, water and energy; urban sprawl onto farmland and habitats; more waste and pollution.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Iran reduced its fertility rate very rapidly in the 1990s.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Through a voluntary family planning programme, free contraception and female education, TFR fell from about 6.5 in the mid-1980s to about 2 by 2000.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Total fertility rate (TFR) in Singapore: 1985: 1.6, 2010: 1.15, 2023: 0.97. Replacement level is about 2.1. Suggest the type of population policy Singapore is likely to need now. Explain your answer.
items.answer: A pro-natalist policy (and/or immigration), because fertility is far below replacement and the population is ageing.
items.markingKey: type [1]; reason [1] [2]

items.stem: Total fertility rate (TFR) in China: 1970: 5.8, 2000: 1.6, 2015: 1.7. Replacement level is about 2.1. (a) State whether the TFR in 2015 is above or below replacement level and explain what this means for future population. (b) Suggest reasons, other than government policy, for the fall in fertility.
items.answer: (a) Below replacement: in the long term the population will decline unless there is immigration (after any population momentum). (b) Female education and employment, urbanisation, lower infant mortality, higher costs of raising children and access to contraception.
items.markingKey: (a) comparison [1]; consequence [1] [2] (b) 1 mark per reason up to [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “The Green Revolution supports Boserup’s ideas.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. High-yielding varieties, irrigation and fertilisers greatly increased food production as population grew.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Table 5.5 shows ecological footprint and biocapacity per person (global hectares, gha): Brazil footprint 2.6, biocapacity 8.6; Bangladesh footprint 0.8, biocapacity 0.4; Japan footprint 4.6, biocapacity 0.6. World biocapacity is about 1.6 gha per person. Suggest two limitations of the ecological footprint as a measure.
items.answer: It uses averages that hide inequality; it simplifies impacts into area; it omits some pollution and biodiversity loss; data quality varies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: “The world is overpopulated.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? Refer to examples you have studied. In your answer you should consider: Malthus and Boserup; ecological footprint; consumption.
items.answer: For: Humanity’s ecological footprint exceeds biocapacity by about 70%; biodiversity loss, climate change and water stress suggest limits are being exceeded. Against: Food production has kept pace with population (Boserup); the problem is unequal consumption and distribution; fertility is falling and population may peak this century. Judgement: The world is not overpopulated in terms of numbers alone, but current levels of consumption are unsustainable.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 3 (6-8 marks): detailed, balanced discussion using named examples and data, with a reasoned judgement. Level 2 (3-5 marks): developed points but limited balance or exemplification. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generalised points. [8]
